summary.title: My role as a founder CTO: Year Four
summary.one_liner: A first-time technical founder/CTO's candid account of scaling RevenueCat's engineering team in 2021, the mistakes of over-juggling tasks, and lessons on delegation, hiring, and hiring a VP of Engineering.
keywords: hiring engineers in a competitive market
remote engineering teams across time zones
takeaways: Founders must shift from doing the work to building the company as the startup moves into growth, which requires ruthless delegation.
Hiring is a persistent bottleneck; specialized roles like SREs and engineering managers can take far longer to fill than backend, frontend, or mobile roles.
Hiring a VP of Engineering took about six months and roughly 40 candidate conversations; executive firms and a MOC document helped align on requirements.
Investors, board members and seasoned executives can take work off a founder's plate and give candid feedback.
Protecting personal health and time off matters; the author identifies founder burnout as a major SaaS risk.
summary.summary: Miguel Carranza, CTO and first-time technical founder of RevenueCat, reflects on 2021: the engineering team went from 8 to 17, company size from 19 to 40, and the company expanded to 28 cities and 10 countries. He describes his shifting day-to-day (hiring, project management, brand, SOC 2 preparation, people management, investor relations), admits he was a bottleneck and over-juggling, and explains how a temporary executive-assistant arrangement helped him regain control of his calendar. The post closes with learnings on delegation, hiring difficulty, executives and investors, personal wellbeing, the VP of Engineering search, and 2022 goals such as engineering onboarding and infrastructure reliability.
